record.title: A preprint measures correlated errors across LLM judges and shows when consensus overstates evidence
record.summary: The authors of arXiv:2609.22512 report correlated errors across open-weight and frontier LLM judges. In their main ten-judge open-weight bank, average pairwise error correlation is 0.206 and the variance-based effective ensemble size is 3.51 on 1,133 RewardBench preference pairs; this is not a claim about majority-vote accuracy. In resampled 100-pair Focus panels, a pooled-vote significance test disagrees with an item-level test in 28% of panels. Three cross-provider frontier judges show error correlation of 0.56 on RewardBench, based on a small bank and relatively few residual errors. The authors find that different error structures favor different filters, while their tested dependence-aware filters do not outperform plain majority on the screened factuality and code settings. These are preprint results, not independently reproduced findings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On 1,133 RewardBench pairs answered by its ten-judge open-weight bank, the paper reports mean pairwise error correlation 0.206 and variance-effective ensemble size 3.51; the authors explicitly state that effective size does not predict majority-vote accuracy or imply that 3.5 judges can replace the bank.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across resampled 100-pair RewardBench Focus panels, a pooled-vote test that treats votes as independent finds significance while an item-level test does not in 28% of panels; the paper reports 22% for Factuality and at most 2% for Math and Precise IF.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For three cross-provider frontier judges on 400 RewardBench pairs, the paper reports mean pairwise error correlation 0.56 and effective size 1.41; its appendix notes that outside Gemini it evaluates only one flagship judge per provider and that estimates use relatively few residual errors.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In tested preference tasks, different shared-error patterns favor different aggregation filters; the authors report that none of 11 screened factuality/code settings met all criteria for a dependence-aware filter to beat majority, and no single filter consistently outperformed majority.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish the natural prevalence of controlled dependence regimes, universal judge dependence, or that its numerical estimates transfer unchanged to other judge banks and tasks.

evidence_gaps.description: the research desk did not independently reproduce the reported error-correlation, effective-size or significance-test estimates.
The paper does not measure natural prevalence for its controlled global co-failure and vulnerable-subgroup interventions; position bias is the main shared vulnerability studied in depth.
Numerical estimates may not transfer to substantially different or larger judge banks, tasks, or changing proprietary frontier models; frontier comparisons use few models and residual errors.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported dependence patterns generalize to deployed evaluation banks, treating judge votes as independent can overstate statistical certainty and distort model comparisons or preference-data filtering. This preprint measures specific banks and datasets, while natural prevalence and transfer to other tasks remain unknown.
limitations: All numerical results are author-reported in one preprint; the research desk did not run code or reproduce them.
The main open-weight bank has ten logical judges from five 7–9B models. The paper says its effective ensemble size is a variance-based summary, not majority-vote accuracy or a replacement count.

The frontier cross-provider comparison covers three flagship judges and 400 RewardBench pairs; outside Gemini, the authors evaluate one flagship judge per provider, and residual-error counts are small.

Controlled global and subgroup failure injections isolate mechanisms but do not estimate their natural prevalence. Position bias is the shared vulnerability measured in depth; other failure structures may differ.
Dependence-aware filters and the selector require trusted calibration labels; the paper reports approximately 100 labels for key procedures and says no tested filter consistently beats majority.

The GRPO comparison uses one seed, three base models and 100 training steps on about 200 pairs from the calibration set, so it is not fully held out and does not show that preference optimization generally reduces dependence.
The authors caution that estimates should not transfer unchanged to substantially different judge banks or tasks, and proprietary models may change over time.
brief.summary: The authors of arXiv:2609.22512 report correlated errors across open-weight and frontier LLM judges. In their main ten-judge open-weight bank, average pairwise error correlation is 0.206 and the variance-based effective ensemble size is 3.51 on 1,133 RewardBench preference pairs; this is not a claim about majority-vote accuracy. In resampled 100-pair Focus panels, a pooled-vote significance test disagrees with an item-level test in 28% of panels. Three cross-provider frontier judges show error correlation of 0.56 on RewardBench, based on a small bank and relatively few residual errors. The authors find that different error structures favor different filters, while their tested dependence-aware filters do not outperform plain majority on the screened factuality and code settings. technical.claimed_result: The authors report mean pairwise error correlation 0.206 and variance-effective size 3.51 for a ten-judge bank on 1,133 RewardBench pairs; pooled-vote versus item-level significance disagreement in 28% of resampled 100-pair Focus panels; and correlation 0.56/effective size 1.41 for three cross-provider frontier judges on 400 RewardBench pairs. They also report that dependence-aware filters are regime-specific and none of 11 screened factuality/code settings met their criteria for beating majority.
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors report approximately 20,000 UltraFeedback votes plus RewardBench calibration and 10,932 controlled co-failure votes; open-weight judge inference used two TITAN RTX GPUs. Downstream dependence/filter analyses operate on recorded vote matrices and do not require additional model inference.
technical.demonstrated_result: The full preprint documents judge banks, datasets, protocols, statistical analyses and author-reported outcomes. the research desk did not execute the released analysis or reproduce the findings.
technical.mechanism: The paper measures correlations between judges' error indicators on trusted labeled pairs, summarizes dependence using a design-effect effective ensemble size, and compares pooled-vote inference with item-level inference. It distinguishes global co-failure from vulnerable-subgroup failures, tests CorrFilter and Bias-Cluster at matched retention, and evaluates a selector using calibration examples. The procedures do not remove judges or change their votes.
technical.regime: Preference judging on RewardBench v2, UltraFeedback and PKU-SafeRLHF, with a ten-logical-judge open-weight bank and separate frontier banks. Additional tests use controlled failure injections, eight external factuality components, and a limited code/factuality screen. Results are regime- and bank-specific.
technical.reproducibility: Appendix C describes datasets, fixed randomization, paired bootstrap procedures and open-weight inference on two TITAN RTX GPUs. The authors state implementation details and analysis code will be released; the research desk did not inspect or run a code repository in this review.
technical.strongest_baseline: Plain majority voting, item-level uncertainty estimates, and the paper's matched-retention supermajority are the relevant baselines. Which filter ranks best changes with the error pattern; no dependence-aware method consistently beats majority.

brief.title: A preprint measures correlated errors across LLM judges and shows when consensus overstates evidence
brief.why_it_matters: LLM-judge agreement is often treated as multiple independent signals in model evaluation and preference-data pipelines. If these reported patterns replicate, vote counts can overstate statistical evidence, and a single aggregation rule may fail when error structure changes. The paper also gives counterexamples to simple remedies: measured correlation alone misses some subgroup failures, and the tested filters do not consistently improve on majority voting. Its estimates remain specific to evaluated judges, tasks and calibration regimes.
